title: A Non-Photorealistic Lighting Model for Automatic Technical Illustration
authors: Amy Gooch, Bruce Gooch, Peter Shirley, Elaine Cohen
key_findings: Observed in technical illustrations: edge lines (boundaries, silhouettes, discontinuities) drawn in black; matte objects shaded with intensities far from black or white, warmth/coolness indicating surface normal; single light gives white highlights; cast shadows usually not shown.

Core idea: if black edge lines and white highlights are drawn, shading must stay in the mid-tones or the lines and highlights get lost; hue shift (cool to warm) carries orientation instead of a large luminance range.

Model: I = ((1+l.n)/2) k_cool + (1-(1+l.n)/2) k_warm, with k_cool = k_blue + alpha*k_d and k_warm = k_yellow + beta*k_d; shown with b=0.4, y=0.4, alpha=0.2, beta=0.6 and also b=0.55, y=0.3, alpha=0.25, beta=0.5 - authors say exact values are not crucial.
Objects keep their colour name under tone shading, so colour can still code categories.
Metal convention: alternating dark/light anisotropic bands, used by illustrators even for smooth metal.
Light placed up and to the right because vision assumes light from above (cited, not tested here).
practical_applications: Cool-to-warm shading for any lined illustration: shadows go to cool hue, lit side to warm, never to black.
Reserve pure black for lines and pure white for highlights; clamp fills to mid-tones.
Metal glasses frames in line art: banded light/dark stripes along the frame.
limitations: Exploratory model, no user study; claims about shape perception lean on cited perception studies.
Hue shift can interfere with albedo (true colour) perception - authors accept this for illustration.

title: Suggestive Contours for Conveying Shape
authors: Doug DeCarlo, Adam Finkelstein, Szymon Rusinkiewicz, Anthony Santella
key_findings: Suggestive contours = lines on visible parts of a surface where a true contour would appear with a small change of viewpoint (zero crossings of radial curvature, filtered for stability).
Contours alone convey limited shape; adding suggestive contours makes sparse drawings easier to read - argued from images, not from a user study.
Artists draw view-dependent lines: a nose in profile gets a ridge line, in front view lines on the sides of the nose.
Not all viewpoints are equal - some views produce much clearer drawings.
practical_applications: In minimal line art, add a few short lines where the form is about to turn away (side of nose, under cheek, fold of sleeve) instead of outlining every crease.
Pick the camera angle that makes the silhouette informative before adding interior lines.
limitations: Needs good curvature estimates; noisy on scanned meshes.
Effectiveness shown qualitatively; quantitative test came later (Cole2009).

title: Where Do People Draw Lines?
authors: Forrester Cole, Aleksey Golovinskiy, Alex Limpaecher, Heather Stoddart Barros, Adam Finkelstein, Thomas Funkhouser, Szymon Rusinkiewicz
key_findings: Art students drew 3D models to 'convey the shape'; 75% of their line pixels were within 1 mm of another artist's line - strong agreement, especially along occluding contours.
Exterior boundary alone accounted for 35-50% of classified line pixels; interior occluding contours 10-20%.
Most non-contour lines lie on large image-intensity gradients and match CG definitions (apparent ridges, ridges/valleys, suggestive contours); no single definition matches all drawings.
Mechanical models: ridge/valley-like lines dominate the remaining lines; smooth/blobby models: fewer non-contour lines, suggestive contours relatively more.
About 14% of lines were not explained by any local property tested; artists differ in style (one artist had far more unexplained lines).
practical_applications: Line budget: silhouette first (it carries roughly half the lines), then interior occluding contours, then a few ridge/fold lines.
Hard-edged objects (glasses frames, furniture) need crease/ridge lines; soft forms (faces, cloth) need few interior lines.
limitations: 12 models, art students, drawings registered to a faint photoreal prompt - may bias toward shading-based lines.
Grey-scale, single lighting; no colour or cartoon stylisation.

title: How Well Do Line Drawings Depict Shape?
authors: Forrester Cole, Kevin Sanik, Doug DeCarlo, Adam Finkelstein, Thomas Funkhouser, Szymon Rusinkiewicz, Manish Singh
key_findings: Gauge-figure study, about 275,000 surface-normal settings, 12 objects x 6 rendering styles (shaded, human drawing, contours only, apparent ridges, ridges/valleys, suggestive contours).
For some shapes people interpret line drawings almost as well as shaded images; computer line drawings can match artists' drawings.
Contours alone were considerably worse than the other line styles.
Smooth blobby shapes were hard to read even when shaded; errors for the best drawings were still around 35-40 degrees for difficult models; shaded prompts had lower average error.
practical_applications: Outline-only cartoon art reads shape poorly on smooth forms - add a shadow shape or a few interior lines.
For blobby subjects (bodies, cushions, food), give shading or texture, not lines alone.
limitations: Lab task with grey renderings of 3D models; not cartoon characters, colour or story context.
Measures shape reading, not appeal or emotion.

title: Line Drawings from 3D Models: A Tutorial
authors: Pierre Benard, Aaron Hertzmann
doi_isbn: Foundations and Trends in Computer Graphics and Vision; arXiv:1810.01175
key_findings: Tutorial/survey of occluding contours, visibility and stylisation of lines from 3D, plus a survey of other line types and artistic shading.
Occluding contours are the core of line rendering; suggestive contours, apparent ridges and highlight lines extend them; image-space edges from depth/normal buffers are a cheap alternative.
Hatching directions: principal curvature, texture or illumination gradients; perceptual work suggests hatching strokes are read as curvature directions (Mamassian & Landy 1998, as cited).
History: toon shading and contour edges spread into games and films after 2000.
practical_applications: For 3D product renders of glasses: render a normal/depth pass and run edge detection to get clean contours, then composite over a toon-ramp shading pass.
Hatch along the form (cross-contour) when shading by lines.
limitations: Technical; focuses on 3D input; I read the introduction and the shading/hatching sections, not every chapter.

title: Illustrative Rendering in Team Fortress 2
authors: Jason Mitchell, Moby Francke, Dhabih Eng
key_findings: Codified conventions of early-20th-century commercial illustration: warm-to-cool hue shift, shadows go cool not black; saturation rises at the terminator (often reddened); high-frequency detail omitted; interior folds echo silhouette shapes; silhouettes emphasised with rim highlights instead of dark outlines.
Characters designed to be identifiable in pure silhouette; this was used to validate designs.
World textures: painterly, loose visible brush strokes, minimal visual noise and minimal repetition; muted colours dominate with small saturated areas.
Shading: diffuse light warping (half-Lambert then a 1D warp ramp) plus a rim term.
practical_applications: Rim light instead of outline for characters on dark backgrounds.
Silhouette test for every character and product shape.
Keep backgrounds lower in detail and saturation than characters.
limitations: Industry paper for one game; claims about readability come from production experience, not controlled studies.

title: Stylization with a Purpose: The Illustrative World of Team Fortress 2 (GDC 2008 slides)
authors: Jason Mitchell (Valve)
key_findings: Read hierarchy: team (colour) -> class (silhouette, proportions) -> selected weapon.
Value gradient on characters: dark feet to light chest; highest contrast at chest level where the weapon is held.
Character creation order: silhouette -> interior shapes solved with shadow shapes -> model sheet -> 3D.
Half-Lambert: scale the cosine term by 0.5, bias by 0.5 and square, to wrap light around the form.
practical_applications: Put the highest value contrast where the story object is (hands holding glasses, face).
Design interior detail as shadow shapes, not extra lines.
limitations: Slides, not a paper; practitioner claims.

title: What line drawings reveal about the visual brain
authors: Bilge Sayim, Patrick Cavanagh
key_findings: There are no lines around objects in nature, yet line drawings are recognised by infants, people without picture experience and chimpanzees - evidence against a purely cultural account.
Orientation-tuned neurons that evolved for edges respond to lines too, so lines stand in for solid edges.
Lines in a drawing stand for depth or slant discontinuities ('object contours'); drawing shadow borders as lines promotes them to object contours and corrupts the image.
Artists' intuitions go beyond current vision science (perspective article).
practical_applications: Never outline cast-shadow or shading borders with the same black line as object edges - use a shape of colour (cel shadow) or a lighter, coloured line.
In line art, every line should mean an edge, fold or occlusion.
limitations: Perspective/opinion article citing studies, not new data.

title: Simple line drawings suffice for functional MRI decoding of natural scene categories
authors: Dirk B. Walther, Barry Chai, Eamon Caddigan, Diane M. Beck, Li Fei-Fei
key_findings: Scene category (beach, city, forest, highway, mountain, office) decoded from fMRI as well from line drawings as from colour photos, from V1 to PPA and RSC; decoding was above chance, not perfect.
Error patterns for drawings resembled those for photos in PPA/RSC.
Behaviour: removing long contours hurt category matching more than removing short contours - long contours carry global scene structure.
practical_applications: Background line art: keep the long structural lines (horizon, floor/wall edges, big masses) and drop short detail lines first.
A simple line BG is enough to tell 'where' the scene is.
limitations: 10 participants, 6 categories; line drawings traced from photos by trained people.

title: Non-Photorealistic Rendering and the Science of Art
authors: Aaron Hertzmann
key_findings: NPR can serve as a 'third pillar' (simulation) for studying how artists make images and how viewers respond.
Theories must be tested against data, not judged by looking at pictures; Cole et al. 2008 cited as the model.
Line thickness example: stroke thickness proportional to isophote distance, clamped - nearer/less curved forms thicker, consistent with many illustrations (Goodwin et al. 2007).
practical_applications: Treat style rules as testable hypotheses: render A/B versions and measure, rather than trust a rule because it looks right once.
limitations: Position paper.

title: Computer-Generated Watercolor
authors: Cassidy J. Curtis, Sean E. Anderson, Joshua E. Seims, Kurt W. Fleischer, David H. Salesin
key_findings: Catalogue of watercolour effects from artists' practice: dry-brush, edge darkening, backruns, granulation and pigment separation, flow patterns, glazing.
Edge darkening: pigment migrates to the edge of a wet area as it dries, leaving a dark rim.
Granulation: pigment settles in the hollows of rough paper, strongest when the paper is very wet; varies by pigment.
Glazing = thin transparent layers over dry layers; layers composited optically with the Kubelka-Munk model.
practical_applications: To fake watercolour in HTML/SVG: transparent fills (multiply), a darker rim at the edge of each shape, paper grain modulating opacity, and a few backrun blooms.
Prompt words that map to real effects: 'edge darkening, granulation on cold-press paper, soft backruns, transparent glazes'.
limitations: Physical simulation, heavy; effects list is the transferable part.

title: Learning to Cartoonize Using White-box Cartoon Representations
authors: Xinrui Wang, Jinze Yu
key_findings: From observing cartoon painting and consulting artists, cartoon images are decomposed into: surface (smooth low-frequency colour, edges/details ignored), structure (sparse flat colour blocks, celluloid style), texture (high-frequency contours and details).
Common features of cartoon images: global structure of sparse colour blocks; details outlined by sharp clear edges; flat smooth surfaces.
Different workflows weight these differently (some palette-led, some colour-block-led).
practical_applications: A cartoon look = flatten colour into a few blocks + smooth surfaces + keep only clear edges; control each separately.
Code is CC BY-NC-SA (non-commercial) - do not use the model commercially; use the idea.
limitations: GAN method trained on anime frames; user study scale small.
license: CVF open access (paper); code CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

title: CartoonGAN: Generative Adversarial Networks for Photo Cartoonization
authors: Yang Chen, Yu-Kun Lai, Yong-Jin Liu
key_findings: Cartoon styles have high simplification and abstraction; cartoon images have clear edges, smooth colour shading and relatively simple textures.
These traits break texture-statistics style losses; an edge-promoting adversarial loss was needed to keep clear edges.
practical_applications: When FLUX output looks 'painted not cartoon', the missing ingredients are usually clear edges and flatter shading - ask for them explicitly.
limitations: Trained on specific anime directors' films; describes features, not perception.

title: Locally Controllable Stylized Shading
authors: Hideki Todo, Ken-ichi Anjyo, William Baxter, Takeo Igarashi
key_findings: The canonical toon shader often creates unwanted shadow areas (e.g. a dark patch over an eye) from geometry or lighting complexity.
Directors want to remove some dark areas and add fictive ones (shade under an eye for fierceness, under the nose for depth) - shadow shapes are designed, not physically computed.
Paint-brush local edits integrated with global lighting and animated smoothly between keyframes.
practical_applications: Cel shadow shapes are a design layer: delete shadows that cover eyes/mouth, add small designed shadows for expression.
For SVG puppets, draw shadow shapes per pose instead of computing them.
limitations: Technical tool paper; artistic rationale from production (OLM Digital).

title: The Role of Book Features in Young Children's Transfer of Information from Picture Books to Real-World Contexts
authors: Gabrielle A. Strouse, Angela Nyhout, Patricia A. Ganea
key_findings: Highly iconic (realistic) pictures help young children link book depictions to real objects; cartoons were the hardest for transfer in the reviewed studies, improving with age.
Simcock & DeLoache 2006 (as cited): 18-month-olds imitated actions from photo books more than from colour drawings; colour drawings worked by 24 months, black-and-white line drawings by 30 months.
Anthropomorphised animals and fantastical content can make it harder for children to separate facts that generalise from story-only features.
practical_applications: For teaching real facts to small children (eye care, real objects), use more realistic depiction; cartoon stylisation is fine for story and emotion with older audiences.
For adult audiences this effect is not shown - do not overgeneralise.
limitations: Review of toddler/preschool studies; not about adults, ads or social media.

title: Transfer between picture books and the real world by very young children
authors: Patricia A. Ganea, Megan Bloom Pickard, Judy S. DeLoache
key_findings: As described by Strouse2018: 15- and 18-month-olds extended a new word from a book to the real object more readily when the book had realistic drawings or photos rather than cartoons.
practical_applications: Same as Strouse2018.
limitations: Not read; only secondary description.

title: XDoG: An eXtended difference-of-Gaussians compendium including advanced image stylization
authors: Holger Winnemoller, Jan Eric Kyprianidis, Sven C. Olsen
key_findings: Extended DoG edge operator with soft thresholding gives line, pencil-shading, pastel, hatching and woodcut looks from one operator.
Canny gives lines whose thickness is independent of edge scale (looks mechanical); DoG lines vary in thickness with edge scale, closer to drawn lines.
Also produces negative edges, ghosting, speed-lines, indication and abstraction effects.
practical_applications: To turn a FLUX/photo background into line art: DoG/XDoG (OpenCV GaussianBlur difference + threshold) rather than Canny for a hand-drawn line feel.
limitations: Image-based; lines follow intensity edges, not object meaning (see SayimCavanagh2011 on shadow edges).

title: Stylized Rendering Techniques for Scalable Real-Time 3D Animation
authors: Adam Lake, Carl Marshall, Mark Harris, Marc Blackstein
key_findings: Real-time cartoon shading via a 1D texture indexed by the Lambertian term, simulating the limited palette of painted cels; pencil-sketch variant; silhouette inking (per indexed abstract and as summarised in Mitchell2007_TF2).
A few bright texels at the lit end of the ramp give a view-independent pseudo-highlight (per Mitchell2007_TF2).
practical_applications: Toon ramp = posterise the light term into 2-3 bands; in SVG use feComponentTransfer type='discrete'.
limitations: Original paper not read; content from abstract index and a citing paper.

title: X-Toon: An Extended Toon Shader
authors: Pascal Barla, Joelle Thollot, Lee Markosian
key_findings: Extends the 1D toon ramp to a 2D lookup indexed by light and a second attribute (depth, orientation) to get level-of-abstraction, aerial perspective, depth-of-field, backlighting and specular effects (search summary of abstract).
Fresnel-like term gives a hard 'virtual backlight' = rim light (per Mitchell2007_TF2).
practical_applications: Depth-based abstraction: farther objects get fewer tone bands, lower contrast and lighter values - a rule for cartoon backgrounds.
limitations: Abstract/summary only.

title: Stylized Highlights for Cartoon Rendering and Animation
authors: Ken-ichi Anjyo, Katsuaki Hiramitsu
key_findings: Highlight shader for cel animation: starts from a Blinn specular shape, then artists translate, rotate, split and square the highlight shape per keyframe; animated automatically without texture maps (per search summary of abstract).
practical_applications: Cartoon highlights are designed shapes (squares, bars, split dots) - in SVG draw them as separate shapes on top, keyed per pose.
limitations: Abstract only.

title: GuiltyGearXrd's Art Style: The X Factor Between 2D and 3D (GDC 2015)
authors: Junya Christopher Motomura (Arc System Works)
key_findings: Custom cel shaders plus 3D models built specifically for those shaders; in-engine shader editor for iteration (search snippet of handout).
Cel shading is hard because a surface is either lit or not; a tiny change in surface normal can create a large shadow blotch (search snippet).
practical_applications: In cel shading, shadow shapes must be art-directed (edit normals or paint shapes) - same lesson as Todo2007.
limitations: Handout not reachable this session; only search snippets.

title: Surface versus edge-based determinants of visual recognition
authors: Irving Biederman, Ginny Ju
key_findings: As cited by SayimCavanagh2011 and Gooch1998: line drawings of objects are recognised about as fast and accurately as colour photographs; surface colour/texture plays a secondary role in fast recognition of intact objects (per secondary summaries).
practical_applications: Clean line art is enough for fast object recognition at feed-scroll speed; colour serves mood and category, not recognition.
limitations: Not read; objects with diagnostic colour (fruit, food) may depend more on colour - later work debated this.

title: Understanding Comics: The Invisible Art
authors: Scott McCloud
key_findings: 'Amplification through simplification': cartooning focuses on chosen details rather than just removing detail; the simpler the icon the more universal (per secondary summaries).
Picture plane triangle: realistic - iconic - abstract.
Widely cited but debated; theoretical, not empirical.
practical_applications: Simple faces (Mint & Tao) invite projection; render settings and objects more fully when they must feel real ('masking' idea - craft claim).
limitations: Book not read this session; claims about identification are untested craft theory.

title: Redesigning Animation: United Productions of America (chapter: UPA Films as Case Studies for a Simplified Visual Language in Animation)
authors: Cinzia Bottini
key_findings: Book and chapter exist (CRC/Taylor & Francis); chapter title frames UPA films of the 1940s-50s as case studies of a simplified visual language influenced by modernist painting, graphic design and poster advertising (per publisher listing and search summaries).
practical_applications: Flat TV-style backgrounds descend from modernist graphic design: shapes and colour fields, not rendered space.
limitations: Only listing seen; no content read.

title: The Vital Background Art: Interview with Background Company Studio Pablo Vol. 1
authors: Otaku Mode (interview)
key_findings: Anime background pipeline: art director sets world style -> art setting (line drawing, 'blueprint of the stage') -> art board (coloured version shared with staff) -> final backgrounds painted from the art board -> art director check.
A 30-minute episode has about 250-400 cuts; about 70-80% need new backgrounds (about 180-300 images); reuse ('multi-use' backgrounds) decided at storyboard to save time for key cuts.
practical_applications: Make one line 'art setting' and one colour 'art board' per location, then generate all angles from them (matches STYLES.md 'write the place once').
limitations: Interview with one company; year 2013 inferred from the page id timestamp (0x51b76057 = June 2013), not printed on the page.

title: Filmmaking Process: Layout
authors: Walt Disney Animation Studios
key_findings: Layout turns storyboards into the first full staged version: lenses, camera moves, angles, composition, how shots cut; requires cinematography, staging and rough animation.
Layout finaling after animation: camera polish, framing, focus, continuity.
practical_applications: Decide camera, horizon and floor line (layout) before painting or generating a background.
limitations: Brief studio page; 3D pipeline.

title: Ben Day Dots Part 8: 1930s to 1950s - the Golden Age of Comics
authors: Guy Lawley
key_findings: Golden Age comics (approx. 1938-1955) printed with Ben-Day tints of only 25% and 50% (colourists reported ~20%/40%): 63 colours plus white = 64 (65 counting black); 1948 Craftint names the plates red, yellow and blue.
Colourists marked colour guides with codes (e.g. YR2); separators made the plates; Craftint replaced hand-laid Ben Day for speed.
Some publishers limited the palette further (one avoided yellow tints until 1969, about 32 colours).
Interiors were line art (Ben Day = line etching, not halftone); line and dot irregularities came from etching, press pressure and newsprint, not intention.
practical_applications: A real 'vintage comic' palette = CMY at 0/20-25/40-50/100% combinations only; dots visible in the light tints; slight misregistration and paper yellowing.
Avoid smooth gradients in a retro-comic recipe - they did not exist.
limitations: Expert blog by a comics-printing researcher, not peer-reviewed; I read the first ~65% of the page.
Spot-check C1 2026-11-25: corrected.

title: What's a Risograph? (print guide)
authors: University of Illinois School of Art and Design
key_findings: Riso = stencil duplicator, one colour per pass, bright spot inks; uncoated paper only.
Files are separated into one grayscale image per ink; 100% black prints as 100% of that ink, 90% as 90%.
Ink is rice-oil based and never fully dries (smudges); large 100% areas cause set-off - use 80-90%.
Print light colours (yellow, pink) first, darker (blue, black) last; allow drying between layers.
practical_applications: Digital riso look: 2-3 spot inks as separate grayscale layers combined with multiply, overprint colours where they overlap, slight registration offset, grain.
limitations: One institution's machine guide; misregistration figures (1-3 mm) come from other vendor guides seen only in search snippets.

title: Nail Your Comic Book Artwork With Precision Color Printing
authors: Walsworth Staff
key_findings: RGB shows a wider gamut than CMYK; CMYK cannot reproduce neon colours; RGB-to-CMYK conversion often looks flatter/duller.
Total ink limits differ by press/paper: sheetfed 300% (270% with UV), coldset web 260% offset / 245% groundwood / 235% newsprint, heatset web 310%, digital 320%.
Line screens: coldset 100-133, heatset 133-175, sheetfed 120-200; images at 1.5-2x line screen, 300-350 ppi default.
G7 grey balance and ICC profiles to keep colour consistent across devices; ask for a printed proof.
practical_applications: Design screen-first cartoon colours knowing which ones will die in print (neon pinks, electric blues, saturated greens) and check a CMYK soft-proof before print jobs.
limitations: Printer's blog; numbers are that printer's recommendations.

title: Anime Skin Tutorial: Makeup, Light, Colour, Tones
authors: IntrinsicKayleigh (CLIP STUDIO TIPS)
key_findings: Use coloured shadows, not grey/black (which make skin dull); first shadow cel-shaded in a warm peach; optional second darker shadow; cool shadows in purple/blue.
Soften only the hard edge of the cel shadow with a small blending brush; blending the whole area looks smudged.
Small highlight dots/wavy lines on cheekbone, eyelid, lip, nose side; colour the line art locally (lighter/brighter at lashes, lips, skin lines).
practical_applications: Cel shadow colour = hue-shifted, more saturated darker version of the base, not base + black.
Coloured line art inside skin areas.
limitations: Single practitioner tutorial (date not stated).
